Lake Sibaya

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa's largest coastal freshwater lake is drying up!

Unique Selling Point:
The coastal plains of Northern Maputuland are systematically drying out, most evident in the continuing receding levels of Lake Sibaya in the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, South Africa's only World Heritage Site. The entire area is a unique ecosystem, a complex network of groundwater aquifers, ancient peatlands and coastal dune forests. Researchers have recorded a 4-5m drop in water levels at Lake Sibaya since 2010 and the groundwater is said to be decreasing at about 1m per annum. Unlike other lakes (St Lucia) and dams in the Pongola River, Lake Sibaya is not recovering from the severe drought of 2015/6/7.

The levels of the Lake Sibhayi (Sibaya) have been dropping at an alarming rate since 2000, creating consternation among scientists, conservationists, tourism organisations, local government and surrounding communities. Research and monitoring in the area are contributing greater detail to formulate strategies to help steer the coastal plain away from a looming environmental crisis.


Summary:
The Northern KZN coastal plains is a very unique area. The area contains 60% of South Africa's peatlands, with the Mfabeni swamp in iSimangaliso dating back to 45,000 years back, and is recognised as the world's oldest peat-accumulating wetland. The vegetation of the region is complex and exceptionally diverse.

The lake supplies water to Sodwana, and Mbazwana & Mseleni communities, and it is the rapid expansion of especially Mbazwana that has raised many eyebrows and is easily blamed for the lake's declining levels. The uMkhanyakude District Municipality has as far back as 2015 realised that Lake Sibaya cannot sustain the increasing extraction levels and they have been working on the Jozini scheme, to supply the area water from the Pongola river... but this is making very little progress.

Climate Change has meant that the area receives a lot less rain than historically, and the lake mostly relies on groundwater and the very shallow water table. Unlike other lakes and dams in the area, Lake Sibaya does not have a very big catchment area. So, decreased rainfall and groundwater extraction has a major impact on the lake.

But perhaps the biggest concern for Lake Sibaya's future is commercial forests and illegal plantations. The Mbazwana and Manzengwenya plantations border the lake and were planted in the 1950's. They are government plantations but the land has been returned to the locals, so they benefit greatly from the rental paid by government. And this is huge, considering that Mbazwana is considered to be one of the poorest communities in South Africa. In addition many local tribes and land owners want access to the lucrative timber industry and illegal, unlicensed plantations are sprouting all over the region.




Further information:
The Maputaland Coastal Forest Mosaic contains extensive areas of wetland. Lake St. Lucia covers approximately 350 km2 and is the largest estuarine system in Africa. Lake Sibayi (60 km2) is the largest freshwater lake in southern Africa, separated from the ocean by a narrow dune cordon. The region is floristically diverse and contains a number of species endemic to the area. For this reason the iSimangaliso Wetland Park World Heritage Site was declared in 1999.

Lake Sibaya lies about 60kms south of the Mozambique border in KZN. The lake is about 60km² and 41m deep at it's deepest point. It is said to hold more water than all three dams in the Umgeni river (Midmar, Albert Falls and Inanda), and is about alf the capacity of the Pongolapoort dam. The lake lies in the coastal plane of Maputuland, an area made up of mostly infertile sandy soil.

The iSimangaliso Wetland Authority simply passes the buck to government, blaming the plantations, but in fact the problem (and possible solution) is far more complicated than that. As the authority in charge of managing our only World Heritage Site, they should be planning for climate change mitigation. Plus the plantations have always been there, since long before it was declared a World Heritage Site in 1999.

The plantations are known as the “Money Trees” by the locals as that is their way to access the economy. Although various studies by the Dept of Forestry (and others) have concluded that removing some of the plantations would greatly assist in the restoration of Lake Sibaya, they are stuck between a rock and a hard place. Studies show that at the very least 5km² of plantations should be removed. But in the case of the Manzengwenya plantation, the Dept says that it will no longer be viable if 5km² is removed – the plantation is only 13,000. There also seems to be little law enforcement, and legal plantations are simply ignored by authorities. Drought conditions here are compounded by plantations of eucalyptus that have expanded 35- fold over the past 20 years – from 200 ha in 1990 to nearly 7 000 ha in 2011. This has changed timber production from a minor to a major land use in the area.

The opportunity to create extra income in an area where unemployment is above 40% and many are living in poverty is understandable. But in the longer term, this source of extra income could eat away at the area’s economic and environmental potential, even threatening the survival of subsistence farming. Evidence increasingly suggests that the effect of eucalyptus plantations is significantly more severe on a sandy aquifer than in other catchments, especially when compounded by drought.

Script:



Lake Sibaya
1
V/O
In Northern KZN, nestled in the Maputaland Coastal Plain between dune forests and ancient peatlands, lies our largest natural coastal freshwater lake…
2
LINK at car next to road - coffee
Lake Sibaya is one of our natural gems, and besides its beauty it supports a host of unique ecosystems, local communities and their livelihoods. But the Lake is in trouble...
3
V/O
STRETCHING ACROSS 70km2, Sibaya can hold more water than the Midmar, Albert Falls and Inanda dams in the uMngeni river combined... But today, it faces a dismal future as the lake is rapidly shrinking… In the last 3 decades, the Sibaya has lost almost half its water.
University of KZN researcher, Dr Lulu Pretorius SPECIALISES IN the area’s wetlands and peatlands AND JOINS A GROUP OF EXPERTS IN investigating the lake’s dramatic water loss. With the help of satellite imaging she shows me just how much the landscape has changed.
4
Lulu Pretorius
This is a 1984 image and you can see the lake. So what you can look at is the white ridges on the edges.
5
V/O
A time-lapse SHOWS THE receding water levels AT ITS MOST glaring….the southern basin EVEN separated from the main lake in 2015 when A severe drought GRIPPED THE REGION.
Since 2016 there’s been some reprieve – but the lake continues to drain – rapidly.
6
Lulu Pretorius
Sibaya lake, at the current rate could easily be dry in 10 years’ time. And that’s an extremely scary thought.
7
V/O
Sibaya forms part of the iSimangaliso Wetland Park – a UNESCO World Heritage Site – which draws tourists from all over the globe. The local economy depends on it, says Lungisani Nxumalo, a community development worker and member of Mabasa Traditional Council Authority.
8
Lungisani
That kind of development must be related to the ecosystem, because we're quite sure that we don't have industries and mines, etc, So it's to protect the environment, the nature that we have so that we can create opportunities for the long-term for our society.
9
Karl Prinsloo
I've been coming here since 1996... There was vast amounts of water here. I mean we used to come kiting here, and as I say, massive flatlands of water that go out for 6/700 metres.
10
V/O
Sodwana Bay local, Karl Prinsloo, is our guide for the day, helping us navigate sandy tracks on rural tribal land. After having spent the past decade working abroad, he’s back and astonished by the changes.
11
Karl Prinsloo
I am quite flabbergasted just coming back to these little areas again and seeing how much water has been.... actually there's no more water. And how far that water line is.
12
V/O
Besides being an obvious tourism drawcard, Sibaya is home to KZN’s second largest populations of crocodiles and hippos - just one of the many reasons this lake is conservation worthy.
13
Mark Schapers
It is one of the most unique environments in the world. It is a freshwater lake that was once estuarine. It's one of the few places where you find saltwater species of fish that have adapted to live in freshwater environments.
14
V/O
Hydrologist, Mark Schapers, explains there are also no major rivers flowing into Sibaya - it’s primarily fed by a shallow aquifer - the main freshwater source for the entire region.
15
Mark Schapers
The Maputaland Coastal Aquifer is one of the most significant unconfined primary aquifers in Southern Africa. It’s pristine, and it’s really a high producing aquifer.
16
V/O
But the water table of the entire Maputaland Coastal Plain is dropping fast and Lake Sibaya is simply a symptom of a much bigger dilemma...
17
Lulu Pretorius
It means all the wetlands and all the peatlands are drying up because they are all fed by the same groundwater system in that area.
18
V/O
The region includes various peatlands between the ages of 3,000 and 8,000 years… as well as the oldest active peat-accumulating wetland in the world - an incredible 45,000 years old…
19
Lulu Pretorius
When the water table drops below the peat level the peat dries out - it becomes desiccated and then it’s just pure organic matter and it can ignite very fast, very easy… and it can smoulder for a very long time.
20
V/O
Once a peatland has burnt it loses its ability to store water. So over time the system becomes less and less capable of recharging.
21
Lulu Pretorius
The water table has dropped now, in places up to 20 metres in the past decade or so.
22
Patrick Zikhali
Big problem. No water no nothing.
23
V/O
Patrick Zikhali was born here in 1937 and remembers a time when water was plentiful and a shallow borehole or well would reach the water table.
24
Patrick Zikhali
Everywhere. There was water. There was water. There was water …

No problem.



25
V/O
Collecting water from working boreholes has become time consuming and expensive for a community with very little.
26
Patrick and Karl
Karl: To get water? Is far?

Patrick: Very far.

Karl: How far? Maybe 5 kilometres?

Patrick: More than 5 kilometres.

Karl: for fresh water?

Patrick: Yes.
27
V/O
The people of the region rely on tourism and subsistence farming. The nutrient-poor sandy soil doesn’t lend itself to intensive crop production and veld has a low carrying capacity for cattle. But the one industry that flourishes here, is forestry.
29
Lulu Pretorius
The big benefit of Eucalypts and why it’s so attractive it that it's such a fast-growing tree. So within 10 years you can harvest and get some money for the wood.
30
V/O
Once harvested, the Ecalyptus timber is pulped through a chemical process to extract the valuable cellulose fibres.
31
LINK
So the bulk of the cellulose pulp is exported and used in the production of textiles like viscose and rayon and a range of other products like washing powders, and cosmetics.
32
V/O
There are two state-owned plantations in the vicinity of Lake Sibaya that were established in the 1950’s. But because the Eucalypts thrive in this area, and they offer relatively easy and guaranteed income to landowners, small plantations have mushroomed all over the landscape - many without the necessary water licenses.
33
LINK
Although water consumption figures vary greatly most experts agree that Eucalypts are very thirsty. The amount of water one tree uses depends on many factors – including which side of the fence you're sitting on. Conservatively a tree like this uses about 40l of water per day. One tree. That's about 150,000l of water over a 10-year lifespan.
34
Shapers
We've got thirty thousand hectares under under trees and the problem with trees is you can’t switch them off and particularly eucalypts. They've got a rooting system that just keeps going.
35
V/O
Of course the population has also expanded greatly over the past twenty years, but even so, Shapers says the amount of water used by people is nowhere near the total consumed by forestry.
36
Mark Shapers
The eucalypts and the pines are using one and a half to two orders of magnitude more water than any other contributing factor.
37
V/O
Simply put, this means that the people of the UMKHANYAKUDE DISTRICT use about 1,000 swimming pools of water per day. Conservatively the eucalypts consume 47,000 swimming pools of water - every day.
38
Lulu Pretorius
It's a big economic injection in that area to have Eucalyptus there, especially for small growers. And it becomes a juggling act of how much are people willing to offer up their income – the little bit that they have – to still have access to water.
40
V/O
It is becoming clear that the Maputaland Coastal Plain can no longer support extensive forestry and the Department of Environmental Affairs and Forestry has placed a moratorium on the issuing of water licences for commercial plantations. But it seems some people are desperate and some even ruthless. In our travels we stumbled upon a freshly ploughed field, which subsequent inquiries revealed as an illegal-plantation-in-the-making.
There is talk of replacing Eucalypts with macadamias, but Shapers says this is not a viable long-term solution.
41
Shapers
Macadamias are only slightly less thirsty than a than a eucalypt. The only advantage of macadamia is that it doesn't have this rooting system that's hugely aggressive, that's going to chase the groundwater the whole time. But unfortunately if you're going to grow macadamias it's gonna be a commercial activity. And the first thing people are gonna do is going to say well let's ensure that our crop is productive. Then they're going to put it under irrigation where they had to get the water from the groundwater.
42
V/O
But whatever the solutions are, they need to be put in place with real urgency, says Pretorius.
43
Pretorius
If Lake Sibaya dries up, in time you might look at impacts like saltwater intrusion because now the groundwater level has dropped below sea level and you start getting influx from sea water. And then of course it has a massive impact on tourism in the area. That's one of the reasons why people got here. Isimangaliso Wetland Park is named after all its wetlands, so it kind of defeats the purpose if all the wetlands are dry.








PROMO 1 11”
It’s a on-of-a-kind coastal freshwater lake in the heart of a world heritage site, but it's facing a looming disaster. Why is Lake Sibaya drying up?








PROMO 2 11”
Lake Sibaya is one of Northern KZN’s natural treasures, but its water is disappearing at an alarming rate and there seems to be no easy fix to save it from an imminent catastrophe.








PROMO 3 11”
Lake Sibaya is natural gem and forms part of our iSimangaliso World Heritage Site, but the lake is drying up and the race is on to find viable solutions to avert an impending disaster.


****

But because the Eucalypts thrive in this area, and they offer relatively easy and guaranteed income to landowners, small plantations have mushroomed all over the landscape - many without the necessary water licenses. 33 LINK Although water consumption figures vary greatly most experts agree that Eucalypts are very thirsty. The amount of water one tree uses depends on many factors – including which side of the fence you're sitting on. Conservatively a tree like this uses about 40l of water per day. One tree. That's about 150,000l of water over a 10-year lifespan. 34 Shapers We've got thirty thousand hectares under under trees and the problem with trees is you can’t switch them off and particularly eucalypts. They've got a rooting system that just keeps going. 35 V/O Of course the population has also expanded greatly over the past twenty years, but even so, Shapers says the amount of water used by people is nowhere near the total consumed by forestry. 36 Mark Shapers The eucalypts and the pines are using one and a half to two orders of magnitude more water than any other contributing factor. 37 V/O Simply put, this means that the people of the UMKHANYAKUDE DISTRICT use about 1,000 swimming pools of water per day. Conservatively the eucalypts consume 47,000 swimming pools of water - every day. 38 Lulu Pretorius It's a big economic injection in that area to have Eucalyptus there, especially for small growers. And it becomes a juggling act of how much are people willing to offer up their income – the little bit that they have – to still have access to water. 40 V/O It is becoming clear that the Maputaland Coastal Plain can no longer support extensive forestry and the Department of Environmental Affairs and Forestry has placed a moratorium on the issuing of water licences for commercial plantations. But it seems some people are desperate and some even ruthless. In our travels we stumbled upon a freshly ploughed field, which subsequent inquiries revealed as an illegal-plantation-in-the-making. There is talk of replacing Eucalypts with macadamias, but Shapers says this is not a viable long-term solution. 41 Shapers Macadamias are only slightly less thirsty than a than a eucalypt. The only advantage of macadamia is that it doesn't have this rooting system that's hugely aggressive, that's going to chase the groundwater the whole time. But unfortunately if you're going to grow macadamias it's gonna be a commercial activity. And the first thing people are gonna do is going to say well let's ensure that our crop is productive. Then they're going to put it under irrigation where they had to get the water from the groundwater. 42 V/O But whatever the solutions are, they need to be put in place with real urgency, says Pretorius. 43 Pretorius If Lake Sibaya dries up, in time you might look at impacts like saltwater intrusion because now the groundwater level has dropped below sea level and you start getting influx from sea water. And then of course it has a massive impact on tourism in the area. That's one of the reasons why people got here. Isimangaliso Wetland Park is named after all its wetlands, so it kind of defeats the purpose if all the wetlands are dry. PROMO 1 11” It’s a on-of-a-kind coastal freshwater lake in the heart of a world heritage site, but it's facing a looming disaster. Why is Lake Sibaya drying up? PROMO 2 11” Lake Sibaya is one of Northern KZN’s natural treasures, but its water is disappearing at an alarming rate and there seems to be no easy fix to save it from an imminent catastrophe. PROMO 3 11” Lake Sibaya is natural gem and forms part of our iSimangaliso World Heritage Site, but the lake is drying up and the race is on to find viable solutions to avert an impending disaster. ****

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa's largest coastal freshwater lake is drying up!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The coastal plains of Northern Maputuland are systematically drying out, most evident in the continuing receding levels of Lake Sibaya in the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, South Africa's only World Heritage Site. The entire area is a unique ecosystem, a complex network of groundwater aquifers, ancient peatlands and coastal dune forests. Researchers have recorded a 4-5m drop in water levels at Lake Sibaya since 2010 and the groundwater is said to be decreasing at about 1m per annum. Unlike other lakes (St Lucia) and dams in the Pongola River, Lake Sibaya is not recovering from the severe drought of 2015/6/7. The levels of the Lake Sibhayi (Sibaya) have been dropping at an alarming rate since 2000, creating consternation among scientists, conservationists, tourism organisations, local government and surrounding communities. Research and monitoring in the area are contributing greater detail to formulate strategies to help steer the coastal plain away from a looming environmental crisis.
metadata.Summary: The Northern KZN coastal plains is a very unique area. The area contains 60% of South Africa's peatlands, with the Mfabeni swamp in iSimangaliso dating back to 45,000 years back, and is recognised as the world's oldest peat-accumulating wetland. The vegetation of the region is complex and exceptionally diverse. The lake supplies water to Sodwana, and Mbazwana & Mseleni communities, and it is the rapid expansion of especially Mbazwana that has raised many eyebrows and is easily blamed for the lake's declining levels. The uMkhanyakude District Municipality has as far back as 2015 realised that Lake Sibaya cannot sustain the increasing extraction levels and they have been working on the Jozini scheme, to supply the area water from the Pongola river... but this is making very little progress. Climate Change has meant that the area receives a lot less rain than historically, and the lake mostly relies on groundwater and the very shallow water table. Unlike other lakes and dams in the area, Lake Sibaya does not have a very big catchment area. So, decreased rainfall and groundwater extraction has a major impact on the lake. But perhaps the biggest concern for Lake Sibaya's future is commercial forests and illegal plantations. The Mbazwana and Manzengwenya plantations border the lake and were planted in the 1950's. They are government plantations but the land has been returned to the locals, so they benefit greatly from the rental paid by government. And this is huge, considering that Mbazwana is considered to be one of the poorest communities in South Africa. In addition many local tribes and land owners want access to the lucrative timber industry and illegal, unlicensed plantations are sprouting all over the region.
metadata.Further information: The Maputaland Coastal Forest Mosaic contains extensive areas of wetland. Lake St. Lucia covers approximately 350 km2 and is the largest estuarine system in Africa. Lake Sibayi (60 km2) is the largest freshwater lake in southern Africa, separated from the ocean by a narrow dune cordon. The region is floristically diverse and contains a number of species endemic to the area. For this reason the iSimangaliso Wetland Park World Heritage Site was declared in 1999. Lake Sibaya lies about 60kms south of the Mozambique border in KZN. The lake is about 60km² and 41m deep at it's deepest point. It is said to hold more water than all three dams in the Umgeni river (Midmar, Albert Falls and Inanda), and is about alf the capacity of the Pongolapoort dam. The lake lies in the coastal plane of Maputuland, an area made up of mostly infertile sandy soil. The iSimangaliso Wetland Authority simply passes the buck to government, blaming the plantations, but in fact the problem (and possible solution) is far more complicated than that. As the authority in charge of managing our only World Heritage Site, they should be planning for climate change mitigation. Plus the plantations have always been there, since long before it was declared a World Heritage Site in 1999. The plantations are known as the “Money Trees” by the locals as that is their way to access the economy. Although various studies by the Dept of Forestry (and others) have concluded that removing some of the plantations would greatly assist in the restoration of Lake Sibaya, they are stuck between a rock and a hard place. Studies show that at the very least 5km² of plantations should be removed. But in the case of the Manzengwenya plantation, the Dept says that it will no longer be viable if 5km² is removed – the plantation is only 13,000. There also seems to be little law enforcement, and legal plantations are simply ignored by authorities. Drought conditions here are compounded by plantations of eucalyptus that have expanded 35- fold over the past 20 years – from 200 ha in 1990 to nearly 7 000 ha in 2011. This has changed timber production from a minor to a major land use in the area. The opportunity to create extra income in an area where unemployment is above 40% and many are living in poverty is understandable. But in the longer term, this source of extra income could eat away at the area’s economic and environmental potential, even threatening the survival of subsistence farming. Evidence increasingly suggests that the effect of eucalyptus plantations is significantly more severe on a sandy aquifer than in other catchments, especially when compounded by drought.
